articles.title: In 2005, an Iowa carpenter who never went to college left nearly $3 million in savings; 14 years later, 33 strangers whose education he funded gathered to remember the man they had never met
articles.summary: Dale Schroeder spent 67 years working as a carpenter at the same business in Des Moines, Iowa.
articles.body: Dale Schroeder spent 67 years working as a carpenter at the same business in Des Moines, Iowa. He grew up poor, never went to college, never married and had no children. He lived a simple life, owning only two pairs of jeans and an old rusty Chevrolet truck. But over the years, he quietly saved almost $3 million.When Schroeder died in 2005, his savings were used to create a scholarship fund for small-town Iowa students who wanted to attend college but could not afford it. The fund eventually paid for the college education of 33 people.Fourteen years after Schroeder's death, those 33 students came together to remember the man whose money had changed their lives, even though most of them had never met him. They called themselves 'Dale’s kids' and gathered around his old carpenter’s lunch box to talk about the difference he had made in their lives.Schroeder's friend Steve Nielsen remembered him as a “blue-collar, lunch pail kind of guy”. He said Schroeder went to work every day, worked hard and was frugal. That simple lifestyle allowed him to build savings that he later decided to use to help young people get an education.He wanted to help students like himselfBefore his death, Schroeder went to Nielsen, who was his friend and lawyer, with an idea for his money. Schroeder had never had the opportunity to attend college, but he wanted other young people to have that chance. “He said, 'I never got the opportunity to go to college. So, I'd like to help kids go to college,'” Nielsen recalled.At first, Nielsen did not know how much money Schroeder had saved. When he asked him about the amount, Schroeder told him it was “just shy of $3 million”. “I nearly fell out of my chair,” Nielsen remembered.Schroeder wanted the money to help small-town Iowa children who had the ability and desire to attend college but lacked the money to do so. His friend said the carpenter wanted to help students who were like him and might not have had an opportunity to go to college without his gift.The scholarship fund eventually helped 33 people attend college without having to pay for their education themselves. For the students who received the money, the scholarship became an opportunity they had not expected.A phone call changed Kira Conard’s plansKira Conard was one of the 33 students helped by Schroeder's savings. At the time, she had completed high school with the grades needed to attend college, but her family could not afford it.Conard grew up in a single-parent household with three older sisters. Paying for college for all four children was not an option, she said. She wanted to become a therapist but did not see a realistic way to pay for her education.“It almost made me feel powerless. Like, I want to do this. I have this goal, but I can't get there just because of the financial part,” she said.At her high school graduation party, Conard was preparing to tell her friends that she would not be going to college. Then she received a phone call from someone who told her about Schroeder and the scholarship. “I broke down into tears immediately,” Conard said.The scholarship allowed her to attend college without taking on debt. She later graduated and planned to begin her career as a therapist.For Conard, the story was difficult to believe because the person funding her education was a man she had never met. “For a man that would never meet me to give me basically a full ride to college, that’s incredible. That doesn’t happen,” she said.33 students remembered SchroederThe 33 people who benefited from Schroeder's savings eventually came together as “Dale’s Kids”. By the time they gathered to honour him, many had completed college and moved into careers including medicine, teaching and therapy.Their meeting also marked the end of the scholarship fund. Conard was the last person to receive one of Schroeder's scholarships after the fund had supported 33 students through college.Although Schroeder was no longer alive to meet the people he had helped, his friends and the scholarship recipients continued to remember his decision. His savings, built through decades of carpentry work and a frugal lifestyle, had been used to give the students an opportunity he had never received himself.There was only one condition attached to the gift. Schroeder could not be repaid because he had died, but he wanted the people he helped to continue the gesture in their own lives.“All we ask is that you pay it forward,” Nielsen said. “You can't pay it back, because Dale is gone, but you can remember him and you can emulate him.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2010, Elon Musk funded a 25-kilowatt solar system for an Alabama disaster centre; 108 panels and battery backup were designed to keep it powered when the surrounding grid went down
articles.summary: Elon Musk funded a solar project in Alabama in 2010.
articles.body: Elon Musk funded a solar project in Alabama in 2010. The 25-kilowatt system, installed at the South Bay Communities Alliance (SBCA) Hurricane Response Center in Coden, Alabama, was designed to help the facility keep operating if a disaster knocked out the surrounding electricity grid. The installation included 108 photovoltaic panels and battery backup and was expected to provide about 90% to 100% of the centre’s electricity needs. Musk’s foundation provided the funding, while solar company SolarCity donated and installed the system. The project came as Coden was still dealing with the effects of Hurricane Katrina and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which had affected the coastal community’s commercial fishing industry.Musk said the project was intended to help residents while demonstrating an alternative to dependence on oil. “This seemed like a good thing to do to help people out, while simultaneously creating awareness that there was a better way to keep things going than just ‘drill, baby, drill,” said Musk, who also runs the electric car company Tesla Motors.A solar system for a community recovering from disastersCoden was a coastal community where commercial fishing had been an important source of employment. The Deepwater Horizon disaster added another setback to an area that was already recovering from Hurricane Katrina. More than 100 families in the community were still waiting to rebuild their homes after the hurricane.The SBCA Hurricane Response Center served as a gathering and response point for the local community. The solar installation was intended to keep the centre powered during emergencies, when a damaged grid could leave residents without electricity.The system was also expected to reduce the centre’s regular electricity costs. “Electricity bills are a big deal for a community center like ours when you have to pay for it out-of-pocket,” says Zack Carter, an organiser for SBCA. “But all of a sudden now we have solar power! For a little area that no one has ever heard about, that’s amazing.”The battery backup was important because this project was more than just producing power in the normal way. It was supposed to provide energy security if a hurricane or other disaster knocked out the local power grid.The project led to wider solar effortsThe Coden installation became an early disaster-relief project involving SolarCity and the Musk Foundation. The organisations later worked on a similar solar project in Japan following the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster. In 2012, SolarCity also worked with partners to provide portable solar power stations for communities affected by Hurricane Sandy.By then, SolarCity’s philanthropy had expanded well beyond disaster relief. In 2013, the company launched the GivePower Foundation to provide electricity to schools in developing countries without reliable power.By 2014, GivePower said it had helped 511 schools in Africa and Central America, exceeding its original target of 400 schools. Its projects used solar panels, batteries and lights, while teams also trained local residents to troubleshoot the equipment and maintain the systems.The organisation's projects included schools in Mali, Nicaragua and Kenya. In Kenya, a school in the village of Kirindon could use laptops donated by Intel after receiving a solar installation.For Coden, however, the original project had a more immediate purpose. The combination of 108 solar panels and battery storage was intended to give a disaster response centre a source of electricity that could continue working even when the surrounding grid could not.​You use AI every day. articles.title: The midnight rescue of Karachi's Mahatma Gandhi
articles.summary: One of the first things I did when I returned to Pakistan in early 2000, this time as the Indian High Commissioner, was to pay my respects to an imposing
articles.body: One of the first things I did when I returned to Pakistan in early 2000, this time as the Indian High Commissioner, was to pay my respects to an imposing bronze statue of Mahatma Gandhi. One of only two Gandhi statutes in Pakistan, Bapuji stands tall at the lobby of the Indian High Commission in Islamabad, famed walking stick in hand, gazing into the distance.The tale of how a pre-Partition statue found its way to its eventual home in the Indian High Commission is a fascinating saga reflecting the tangled tumultuous history of our two countries. It is a journey in which I was honoured to have played a small part.According to several accounts, the statue originally stood outside the Sindh high court on what was known as Kings Way in Karachi. It had been commissioned by the Indian merchant association sometime in the 1930s to commemorate the historic Karachi session of the Indian National Congress. The plaque underneath the life-size monument apparently read: “Mahatma Gandhi – the reputability of freedom, truth and nonviolence.”Partition brought the inevitable dislocation. With communal riots engulfing Karachi in 1948, there was fear that the statue would be torn down amidst mob fury. Accounts vary on what exactly happened, but apparently after the intervention of Jamshed Nussranwanji Mehta, a Parsi and former Mayor of Karachi, the statue was surreptiously taken down and moved quietly to the home of the Cowasjees, a leading Parsi family of Karachi.And there it lay for more than thirty years…A few months into my first stint in Pakistan as Consul General in Karachi, a middle aged Parsi gentleman approached me. He was a well known Karachi businessman, activist and columnist whose name I am withholding. Over the course of several meetings he told me his incredible tale. How he as a young man along with several of his school chums insouciantly removed the Gandhi statue in the dead of the night armed with some basic tools and a lorry – all while Karachi seethed with fear and hatred. It was then ferried to his father’s home, initially meant as a temporary abode until a handover to Indian representative could be organised. Unfortunately, the then Indian High Commissioner to the Dominion of Pakistan could not assure a safe passage and refused. And that was how the Cowasjees became the involuntary guardians of Gandhi in PakistanThe Parsi gentleman was clear that his part in the story had to come to an end. We were now in the early 1980’s. General Zia’s Islamisation project was well underway. Sharia laws had been introduced into the legal system. Strict Islamic punishments were to be meted out for crimes like adultery, theft and drinking of alcohol. Educational curriculums were being rigorously overhauled to promote religious studies and conformity with orthodox Islamic principles. Dress codes, especially for women, were being enforced. The sari, once common amongst upper class Pakistani women, was fast disappearing. An ongoing media clampdown weeded out content deemed as un-Islamic.Though historically Parsis, unlike other minorities in Pakistan, have enjoyed a somewhat protected status and though Ardeshir was and continued to be a fearless and outspoken critic of the political establishment, he was no longer comfortable with his role as the statue’s custodian. He asked me if the long delayed handover of the statue could finally take place.I immediately agreed. I was determined that the statue, now a priceless historical artifact, should come home on my watch. There was, however, a tricky logistical issue to navigate. Constant surveillance by Pakistani intelligence was a fact of life. So how could we transport the statue without compromising the Cowasjees.After clearance from Delhi, we decided to replicate the original midnight run. A non-descript truck, organised by the Consulate, picked up a large wrapped item from the Cowasjee residence and quietly brought it to the Indian mission late one summer night.I personally inspected the precious cargo. Through all its travails, the statue had endured some damage. One hand was broken and the glasses were cracked, but otherwise Gandhiji stood tall. We arranged for some minor repairs, and after a few weeks, the statue took pride of place in the Chancery reception. Suddenly confronted with this majestic but serene statue, surprised Pakistani visitors were often curious about its origins, but we remained tightlipped.Eventually, once the statue was properly restored, we arranged for its transportation to the High Commission in Islamabad. In hindsight, that last trek from Karachi to Islamabad turned out to be as consequential as the original journey in 1948. In 1993, following the demolition of the Babri Masjid, furious mobs in Pakistan attacked over 30 Hindu temples and in Karachi ransacked both the Consulate and the Consul General’s residence in which I had once lived. Valuable art was vandalised, including a beautiful painting by B. Prabha.Post the 1993 attacks, the Indian consulate in Karachi closed down. It remains shut to this day. In Islamabad, however, the Gandhi statue still stands, an enduring testament to “freedom, truth and non-violence” true to its original plaque.G. Parthasarathy has served as India’s Consulate General in Karachi and as India’s High Commissioner in Islamabad.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: For Kolkata’s football fans, Brazil was love before first sight
articles.summary: As the city gears up to host Vini Jr & Co for tomorrow’s friendly, stars of India’s golden era talk of a lifelong romance ignited by match reports and the
articles.body: As the city gears up to host Vini Jr & Co for tomorrow’s friendly, stars of India’s golden era talk of a lifelong romance ignited by match reports and the odd footageFrom Argentine greats Diego Maradona and Lionel Messi to Germany’s Oliver Kahn, Kolkata has hosted some of football’s greatest icons down the years. Yet, the city holds a special place for Brazil, a love affair that began with its first breakout stars and is now set to only deepen when Vinicius Jr and his teammates arrive for the friendly they play against India on Saturday at Salt Lake Stadium.Coach Carlo Ancelotti’s boys are ranked No.6 in world football. India are a distant No.138. Some veterans have commented on the audacity of a lowly-ranked side taking on one of the giants of the game, but when Brazil first captured the imagination of football fans in India, it had more to do with a sense of kinship than purely adulation.Dreaming without visualsBrazil’s rise coincided with India’s emergence as the superpower of Asian football, a golden era — notwithstanding the missed chance of taking part in the 1950 World Cup in Brazil — marked by triumphs at two Asian Games (1951, 1962) and a fourth-placed finish at the 1956 Olympics. As Brazil shook up football with its working-class, mixed-race team playing a unique brand of free-flowing football, India turned to it for inspiration.“During our time, we only wanted to play like Brazil. Because they were the No.1 team and we also wanted to be No.1,” former footballer Shyam Thapa told TOI. “We used to read a lot about Brazil in newspapers and were instantly drawn to this image of a team that might be economically poor like us but had the gift to conjure magic on the field and boss over European elites,” recalls Thapa.This was before the era of live telecast and highlight shows, with imagination filling in the details that reports could not convey. “Remember those were pre-TV days and we didn’t have the opportunity to watch Brazil live. So, we used to visualise their football magic in our own way. When Chuni-da dribbled past with one of his famous body feints, we would marvel at the move, saying it would make even Garrincha proud,” says Gautam Sarkar, a star footballer of the 1970s, referring to Indian legend Chuni Goswami and the Brazilian master considered to be among the greatest dribblers of the game.“In my mind, I discovered my Brazil through Kajol Mukherjee’s control and touch, Bengal Nagpur Railway star Rajendra Mohan’s running with and without the ball and, later, in Surajit Sengupta’s artistry,” adds Sarkar.But it wouldn’t be long before Kolkata found it could put faces to the names that set the city’s football pulse racing.Coach Datta’s ProjectorAmal Datta’s career as a footballer never matched the ripples he would later create in his coaching avatar. Giving up his playing career prematurely to travel to England for a one-year FA coaching course, he returned in 1960 with a certificate that made him India’s first professional coach. In his luggage was a projector and grainy video clips that would give many in the city their first glimpse of Pele, Garrincha, Didi, Vava and Zagallo en route to winning the 1958 and 1962 World Cup finals.“Amal-da’s clippings on the projector screen became an absolute craze in the city during the 1960s. He also used to tell the audience to focus on and study the Brazilians’ movements on and off the ball,” recalls Sarkar.Then, in the 70s, came the documentary called, ‘Giants of Brazil’. “When it was screened for the first time at Lighthouse cinema, it resonated profoundly with the public,” says Gautam Roy, a football statistician. “Reading about Brazilian football and their artistes in newspapers and magazines was the sole source for firing our imagination. But seeing the documentary just drove up the craze,” he adds, noting how the hype would go on to hit stratospheric levels during Pele’s 1977 visit.Pele Comes CallingWhen Pele and his New York Cosmos club came calling, two of India’s top club sides presented a picture of contrasts. For Mohun Bagan, the club synonymous with awakenings of national pride, those were turbulent times. Their city rivals, East Bengal, had emerged as the undisputed rulers of Indian football and were still basking in the glow of their 5-0 thrashing of Bagan in the IFA Shield final of 1975.But, in 1976, Bagan general secretary Dhiren Dey pulled off a coup by snatching a host of players from East Bengal. It was around the same time that he learnt of Cosmos’s proposed tour of Asia. He quickly chalked out a plan to cash in on the visit. “I had already committed myself to East Bengal when he (Dey) proposed that I play for Bagan and grab the opportunity of taking the field against Pele. It was an offer too tempting for me to ignore,” says Shyam Thapa, who scored in the 2-2 tie against Cosmos at Eden Gardens on Sept 24, 1977.Saturday’s friendly comes at that time of the year when a sense of festivity drifts into Bengal’s air. As Kolkata gears up for Durga Puja, it will also look to embellish a deep bond that beats as part of its footballing heart. For both Sarkar and Thapa, the arrival of the Brazil team is like the journey coming full circle. Whatever the result, they know nothing can take away the bragging rights won nearly 50 years back: “the pride of playing against Pele”.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Gujarat UCC Bill gets President Murmu’s nod paving way for implementation
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: President Droupadi Murmu has given her assent to the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill, 2026, completing the key legal process required for the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: President Droupadi Murmu has given her assent to the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill, 2026, completing the key legal process required for the state to enact the law.The Gujarat assembly had earlier passed the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill, 2026, making the state the second in India after Uttarakhand to pass legislation seeking to implement a Uniform Civil Code. However, the provisions of the bill will not apply to members of Scheduled Tribes (STs).READ ALSO: ‘Sat for 11 seconds’: Mystery shrouds Premanand Maharaj disciple’s death after CCTV footage emergesWhile tabling the bill in the Assembly, chief minister Bhupendra Patel had said that the UCC was among the key reforms that Prime Minister Narendra Modi was determined to implement. "The key aim of introducing the bill is to ensure social harmony and national unity. The Supreme Court has also suggested that UCC will ensure women's rights are secured," the CM said.The bill proposes mandatory registration of marriages and divorces, with a fine of up to Rs 10,000 for non-compliance.It also makes registration of all live-in relationships compulsory, while requiring couples to notify authorities when such relationships end. Children born from live-in relationships will be considered legitimate children of the couple, while women deserted by their live-in partners will be entitled to seek maintenance, according to the bill.The legislation bans polygamy and provides for up to seven years' imprisonment for marriages conducted through coercion or force. Divorce through any means other than a court decree will be punishable with up to three years in prison.The bill also allows divorced couples to remarry without conditions and prohibits the practice of `halala' in certain communities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2014, a Phoenix architect turned a discarded 1955 grain silo into a 340-square-foot home, using its curved shell and a skylight to add a second floor
articles.summary: Discover how architect Christoph Kaiser transformed a discarded 1955 grain silo into a stunning two-story, 340-square-foot home in Phoenix's Garfield Historic District, leveraging its unique design features for modern living.
articles.body: Phoenix architect Christoph Kaiser came across and bought a dismantled 1955 grain silo that was being sold online, and turned it into a 340-square-foot home in the Garfield Historic District of downtown Phoenix. The completed Silo House was designed as a two-story residence built within the silo’s existing steel shell.The silo had originally been built for agricultural use and was far from its eventual home in downtown Phoenix. Kaiser found the dismantled structure online and arranged to bring it to Arizona, where he developed the project as both architect and builder. The finished structure has an 18-foot diameter and 340 square feet of livable space, and Kaiserworks dates the Silo House to 2014.The circular shell provided the exterior walls, while Kaiser inserted a smaller two-story living volume inside it, and that approach meant that the interior had to work around the silo’s curved shape rather than being divided into conventional rectangular rooms. Abitare reported in January 2016 that the structure had been converted into a compact home for two, and its article describes the addition of a second floor above the ground level, reached by a spiral staircase, with custom-made furniture designed around the cylindrical interior.A second floor inside a cylinderThe finished plan placed the living functions within a two-story walnut and black-steel volume along the silo’s southern side, and Kaiserworks says the arrangement was intended to make the most of the available floor area while also preserving a sense of space inside the small footprint. A spiral staircase connects the two levels, and the upper portion accommodates the bedroom, while the lower level contains the main living functions.The cylindrical shell remains visible throughout the house, and instead of covering the original form with conventional walls, the design uses it as part of the interior experience, which allows the curved steel exterior to remain central to the identity of the home. A 2015 article in Modern Steel Construction described the circular footprint as about 190 square feet while noting the larger two-story arrangement inside the silo.The skylight helped cool the homeKaiserworks incorporated subterranean air ducts into the design in order to reduce mechanical noise and help with passive cooling. An operable skylight at the top of the silo works with the ventilation system to move air through the house, and the exterior corrugated shell was also painted white, which helped reflect sunlight.Abitare reported that the skylight was positioned at the top of the silo and that the air ducts worked passively with it, and the design therefore used the original height and cylindrical shape of the agricultural structure as part of the home's climate strategy. The materials inside are deliberately different from the industrial exterior, as walnut and black steel form the main interior elements, with furniture made to fit the available space. The contrast keeps the old agricultural shell visible while the interior functions as a small modern residence.From grain storage to a city homeThe Silo House was completed in 2014, although several architecture publications, including Abitare, covered the project in 2016. ArchDaily also records the project year as 2014 and gives the area as 340 square feet. The silo was originally part of an agricultural setting, but its new life placed it inside Phoenix’s Garfield Historic District.Kaiser retained the steel shell and built an entire residence around its limitations, and used the circular walls, vertical space and roof opening as design features. The result is a home that occupies only 340 square feet but has two levels, a bedroom, living areas, custom furniture and a skylight. The grain silo no longer stores grain, and its original shell now forms the exterior of a small Phoenix residence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1997, Martha Stewart bought Edsel Ford's 63-acre Maine estate for reportedly under $6 million; she restored its historic landscape while preserving the 12-bedroom stone house and Ford family china
articles.summary: Perched above Seal Harbor on Maine’s Mount Desert Island, Skylands carries nearly a century of history tied to the Ford family and is now closely
articles.body: Perched above Seal Harbor on Maine’s Mount Desert Island, Skylands carries nearly a century of history tied to the Ford family and is now closely associated with Martha Stewart. Stewart bought the 63-acre estate in 1997, reportedly for just under $6 million, and has since treated the property as a piece of American architectural and landscape history rather than simply a summer home. In her own Martha Stewart Blog, she described the estate’s history and the work involved in bringing its Jens Jensen-designed landscape back towards its original character.A retreat created for Edsel FordSkylands was developed for Edsel Ford, the son of Henry Ford, and his wife, Eleanor. The house was completed in 1925 and designed by architect Duncan Candler, while renowned landscape designer Jens Jensen created the surrounding landscape. Architectural Digest describes the three-story stone residence as sitting high above Seal Harbor, with a setting shaped by granite outcrops, trees, ferns and terraces rather than a conventional manicured lawn.The estate's design was closely connected to its natural surroundings. Jensen incorporated elements including mossy woods, ferns, evergreens and maples into the landscape, creating a setting that blended the house with the terrain around it.In a 2013 post on her blog, Stewart wrote that the Ford estate had been sold to another family and said the property had not been maintained in the same way as it had been during the Fords’ ownership. When she purchased Skylands in 1997, she brought in landscape architect Patrick Chassé to help with the restoration of Jensen’s work. Stewart wrote that Chassé helped with the design of a council ring while also addressing the “challenges and compromises” involved in bringing the historic landscape back to its natural character.Stewart preserved the house rather than remaking itThe character of Skylands has remained closely tied to its original architecture. Architectural Digest reported that the house has 12 bedrooms, several outbuildings and a 60-foot-long beamed living hall. Rather than extensively modernising the property, Stewart embraced many of its existing details and furnishings. The property was sold to Stewart with much of its contents still inside. According to Architectural Digest, the purchase included cabinets and shelves containing the Fords’ silver, glassware, china and linens. Stewart herself told the magazine, “I didn’t have to buy a plate,” adding that she had nevertheless added her own pieces over the years. That approach helped retain a direct connection to the home's previous owners. Architectural Digest noted that Stewart has described herself as a caretaker of the property.Interiors reflect both Ford history and Stewart’s styleInside, Skylands retains numerous details associated with its early-20th-century design. These include Pewabic-tiled bathrooms, leaded-glass windows, polished copper, cut crystal and vintage Frigidaire refrigerators in the kitchen, along with furniture and decorative objects ranging from Georgian stools and wing chairs to regional maps and prewar prints of Maine birds.Stewart has added her own design touches, but they have generally been incorporated alongside the property's existing character. Architectural Digest reported that Kevin Sharkey, then executive editorial director at Martha Stewart Living, assisted her with the decorating. Some original objects have been stored, while others remain part of the home's interiors.The house also became a source of inspiration for Stewart's wider creative work. Architectural Digest reported that she spends part of July and August at Skylands, along with long weekends during other parts of the year, and that the property has served as a setting and inspiration for her design work and media projects.A landscape shaped by historyThe restoration of Skylands has extended beyond the house itself. Stewart's 2013 blog post focused particularly on the work of Patrick Chassé and the challenge of recovering aspects of Jensen's original landscape design. She wrote that Jensen's work had used the existing vegetation and terrain to create a landscape that felt naturally integrated with the property. The estate's history also remains visible in its setting. Architectural Digest described pink-granite gravel drives winding through the forest, terraces surrounded by natural vegetation and a house constructed from local stone that appears to emerge from the surrounding granite landscape.The property had changed hands before Stewart acquired it. Architectural Digest reported that the Fords and their four children spent summers there until another family acquired the estate in 1980, following Eleanor Ford's death. That family subsequently sold Skylands to Stewart in 1997.Today, Skylands remains a private retreat for Stewart, but its significance extends beyond its role as a celebrity home. Its architecture, original furnishings and Jensen-designed landscape preserve links to the Ford family's era on Mount Desert Island. Stewart's approach has centred on maintaining those layers of history while continuing to use the estate as a living home rather than treating it solely as a preserved relic.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 1993, Matera’s once-shunned cave districts became a UNESCO World Heritage site; restored stone homes now host hotels, shops and a living city
articles.summary: Discover how the Sassi districts of Matera transformed from overcrowded caves to a thriving UNESCO World Heritage site, blending history, architecture, and modern life.
articles.body: The Sassi districts of Matera were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 and formally recognised as a settlement of homes, churches, monasteries and workshops that were carved into the rock of southern Italy. The designation came four decades after the Italian government had begun moving residents out of the caves because of overcrowding and poor sanitation.The Sassi are made up of two historic districts called Sasso Caveoso and Sasso Barisano, which were built into the natural rock of the Murgia landscape. UNESCO’s description explains that the World Heritage property covered 1,016 hectares and contained more than 1,000 dwellings, along with shops and workshops. There was evidence of occupation going back to the Palaeolithic period and the text describes the Sassi as an example of a settlement that adapted closely to its terrain and environment.But the ancient appearance of the district concealed serious problems by the middle of the 20th century, as families were living in cramped cave homes, often alongside animals, with inadequate sanitation and limited infrastructure. The Italian government passed legislation that called for the evacuation of the Sassi and the construction of new residential districts in 1952. The relocation continued through the following years, and by 1958 the population had abandoned the caves for newer housing.Empty homes created a new problemThe Sassi were no longer functioning as an ordinary residential district, and abandoned structures began to deteriorate. UNESCO's documentation says that the evacuation interrupted the site's continuous occupation in the 1950s, and also notes that abandonment caused some degradation, while the return of people from the 1980s helped restore the traditional function of the property.The recovery was not simply about repairing old walls, and Italy eventually developed a framework for using parts of the district. Law 771 of 1986 placed the historic area under the direct management of the Municipality of Matera and established urban plans that were aimed at the architectural, urban, environmental and economic recovery of the Sassi. One of those plans specifically emphasised residential development as a way to rehabilitate the area and re-establish a local population.UNESCO recognition came in 1993UNESCO's World Heritage Committee inscribed the Sassi and the Park of the Rupestrian Churches of Matera on the World Heritage List under cultural criteria that covered its historical continuity, architecture and relationship with the surrounding environment in 1993. The property includes churches, monasteries, hermitages and the wider landscape around the historic districts, and UNESCO considers the site to be an outstanding example of a rock-cut settlement that remained closely adapted to its environment over more than two millennia. The Sassi were no longer simply an abandoned part of Matera by then, with restoration and rehabilitation bringing buildings back into use, while residents were gradually returning.From abandoned district to living cityThe modern Sassi now function as part of Matera rather than as a sealed archaeological site, and visitors move through the old cave streets and underground passages, while shops, restaurants and other businesses operate within the historic districts. Italy's official tourism portal describes Sasso Caveoso as an area where ancient cave dwellings remain intact and Sasso Barisano as an area containing shops, while also pointing visitors toward the historic cave houses that show how people lived there before the evacuation.The old cave architecture now forms part of Matera's tourism economy, while the wider district continues to contain residential spaces and everyday urban activity, which creates a different preservation challenge from just protecting an abandoned monument. UNESCO notes that increasing tourism can affect the presentation and atmosphere of the historic property and says that visitor management is necessary. The Sassi therefore remain both a protected heritage site and a functioning part of Matera. The transformation took decades, and the same caves that had been emptied because they were considered unsuitable for modern living became the centre of an international heritage district after restoration, renewed occupation and UNESCO recognition. In 1993, that shift was formally recognised when the Sassi entered the World Heritage List.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2006, a floating-home resident challenged Riviera Beach’s $2.4 billion waterfront redevelopment plan; the city later abandoned it
articles.summary: In 2006, Fane Lozman challenged a $2.4 billion redevelopment plan in Riviera Beach, Florida, leading to landmark legal battles over eminent domain, maritime law, and property rights.
articles.body: In 2006, a small floating home in Riviera Beach, Florida, became central to a larger fight over land, redevelopment and local government power. Fane Lozman had moved his houseboat into the city-owned marina when he discovered that Riviera Beach was planning a $2.4 billion waterfront redevelopment project. The proposal called for acquiring about 2,200 homes and businesses, along with the marina, through eminent domain and transferring the properties to a private developer.According to the University of Miami Law Review, Lozman became an outspoken opponent of the redevelopment plan and challenged the city's actions surrounding the proposed project. Lozman objected publicly to the plan and challenged how the city approved its agreement with the developer. Within months, the redevelopment scheme was abandoned. It developed into a series of court battles that eventually took Lozman and his unusual home to the US Supreme Court.A waterfront redevelopment plan meets a new lawFor several years, Riviera Beach had been pursuing a major redevelopment of its waterfront. The proposed project, estimated at $2.4 billion at the time, was intended to transform the marina area through private development. Plans included commercial and residential properties, as well as facilities for visitors and yachts. The redevelopment was also affected by changes to Florida's eminent-domain laws. State lawmakers passed House Bill 1567 on May 4, 2006, restricting the use of eminent domain for economic-development purposes, and Gov. Jeb Bush signed the legislation into law on May 11. In the middle of this process, on May 10, the Riviera Beach City Council agreed to work with Viking Inlet Harbour Properties as the project's master developer. By November 2006, however, the city had abandoned the waterfront redevelopment scheme.From redevelopment opponent to courtroom defendantLozman’s resistance to the plan led him to attend Riviera Beach City Council meetings frequently. His lawsuit over the development agreement led to further conflict with the city. In one case, Lozman was described as a loudmouth criticising the redevelopment project and alleging wrongdoing by city officials. Later, the city attempted to remove Lozman from the marina. One dispute concerned the terms of his marina residency.The dispute also drew academic attention. As the University of Miami Law Review notes, the redevelopment controversy came before the dispute over Lozman’s floating home and formed part of the background to his ongoing conflict with Riviera Beach. The city later filed a separate federal suit arguing that the floating home was a vessel subject to federal admiralty law. It was a 60-by-12-foot two-story wooden home consisting of a kitchen, bathroom, bedroom, and office space.The floating home reaches the Supreme CourtAccording to the Florida Law Review, the legal significance of the case extended beyond the unusual appearance of Lozman's home. The dispute eventually reached the US Supreme Court, which ruled in 2013 that Lozman's floating home was not a vessel under federal maritime law. The justices said the key question was whether a reasonable observer would see the structure as designed to a practical degree to transport people or things over water. Because the home lacked features associated with maritime transport and was designed as a residence, the court ruled in Lozman’s favour. The decision established a “reasonable observer” test for determining vessel status, though later cases raised questions about how consistently it could be applied.However, Lozman’s legal disputes with Riviera Beach did not end with the 2013 ruling. In 2018, the Supreme Court said the lower court had used the wrong test to evaluate Lozman’s retaliation claim and sent the case back for further proceedings. What began as a dispute over waterfront redevelopment grew into a long legal history involving eminent domain, open-government laws, free speech and maritime law. The $2.4 billion project was abandoned in 2006, but the legal disputes surrounding Lozman’s floating house continued for years and reached the US Supreme Court more than once.You use AI every day. articles.title: Steve Jobs’ son watched his father battle cancer as a child; decades later, Reed Jobs is using a $1 billion fund to fight the disease
articles.summary: Reed Jobs was 12 when his father, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was diagnosed with a rare form of pancreatic cancer.
articles.body: Reed Jobs was 12 when his father, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was diagnosed with a rare form of pancreatic cancer. Eight years later, Steve died at 56, while Reed was an undergraduate at Stanford. The experience shaped Reed’s interest in cancer research, leading him to spend summers working in oncology laboratories as a teenager before eventually moving into healthcare investing. In 2023, he launched Yosemite, an oncology-focused investment firm that combines venture capital with philanthropic funding. Yosemite initially launched with more than $200 million. By early 2026, the firm had raised another $200 million-plus for its second fund and said it was managing more than $1 billion in assets.Reed Jobs’ childhood changed after Steve Jobs’ diagnosisReed became interested in cancer after seeing his father diagnosed when he was 12. Steve Jobs had been diagnosed with a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, a rare form of pancreatic cancer. Reed later spent time working in oncology laboratories at Stanford as a teenager and initially entered Stanford as a pre-med student.Steve Jobs died on October 5, 2011, at the age of 56. Reed was 20 at the time and was studying at Stanford. After his father's death, Reed changed his major from pre-med to history. He eventually returned to healthcare through his work at Emerson Collective, the impact-investing and philanthropic organisation founded by his mother, Laurene Powell Jobs.Before creating Yosemite, Reed spent years working at Emerson Collective, where he focused on health and cancer-related initiatives. Yosemite emerged from that work and became an independent organisation in 2023.The firm announced its first close of more than $200 million in August 2023. Its model combines traditional venture investment with philanthropic grants for academic researchers. The aim is to support scientific work at an early stage and help promising discoveries develop into treatments and companies.Yosemite focuses exclusively on oncology and has invested in areas including gene therapy, immunotherapy, cancer vaccines, radiopharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence-powered drug discovery and earlier cancer detection.Yosemite now manages more than $1 billionYosemite's financial scale has grown substantially since its launch. In January 2026, the San Francisco Chronicle reported that the firm had raised more than $200 million for its second fund and was seeking an additional $150 million. The new fund was backed by institutions and investors including Amgen, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, MIT and John Doerr.Forbes reported that Yosemite's second fund was targeting $350 million. Following its latest funding round, the firm said it managed more than $1 billion in assets, including money overseen for hospitals, endowments and foundations.The firm's own announcement said its second fund had initially closed at more than $200 million and that Yosemite now managed more than $1 billion in assets.Reed Jobs wants cancer to become manageableReed has described a long-term goal of changing how cancer is treated. In an interview reported by the San Francisco Chronicle, he said he believes many cancers could eventually move from being fatal diagnoses to manageable, chronic diseases within his lifetime. Yosemite's current investments reflect that strategy. The firm has backed companies working on technologies ranging from gene therapies and cancer vaccines to AI-assisted drug discovery. According to the San Francisco Chronicle, Yosemite was invested in about 20 companies and expected its new fund to support around 25 companies.The Yosemite name has a personal connectionThe name of Reed's firm also comes from an important chapter in his family's history. Steve Jobs and Laurene Powell Jobs married on March 18, 1991, at the Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite National Park. The ceremony was attended by about 50 people, and the wedding included a vegan cake shaped like Half Dome. The couple also went hiking after the ceremony. Reed was born in September 1991, months after his parents' wedding. He was their first child, followed by daughters Erin and Eve.Reed's career has therefore come full circle. His interest in oncology began during his father's illness, continued through his teenage work in cancer laboratories and later became part of his professional work at Emerson Collective.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Melbourne homeowner bought a house years after construction; water damage he noticed months later became a $176,297 insurance battle
articles.summary: A dwelling completed in Caulfield South on 18 November 2014 later became the subject of a $176,297.76 County Court award.
articles.body: A dwelling completed in Caulfield South on 18 November 2014 later became the subject of a $176,297.76 County Court award. Mr Fall-Armytage became the registered proprietor in May 2018 and, between June and November 2018, noticed water damage, staining, mould and leaking after heavy rainfall. According to Cogent Legal, his domestic building insurance claim, made in August 2023, was refused. The County Court ordered indemnity for 11 defects, plus temporary accommodation and storage costs. In Victorian Building Authority v Fall-Armytage [2026] VSCA 32, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and dismissed the claim, except for the 11th defect, with that defect remitted to the County Court.Why did the $176,297.76 insurance claim become a legal battleMr Fall-Armytage made a claim under the domestic building insurance policy in August 2023, and the claim was refused. The County Court ultimately found in his favour. It ordered that he be indemnified for the cost of rectifying 11 defects, together with temporary accommodation and storage costs. The amount ordered was $176,297.76.The Victorian Building Authority, which had been substituted for the Victorian Managed Insurance Authority by operation of statute, sought leave to appeal. The appeal was confined to a single issue of construction concerning clauses 34 and 35 of the policy. The policy covered the insured where the insured could not recover from the builder because of insolvency, death or disappearance. Clause 32 was the primary indemnity provision, covering loss or damage sustained by the insured in those circumstances. Clauses 34 and 35 dealt with the duration of cover, with clause 34 addressing non-structural defects and clause 35 addressing other causes.What did the court decide about when building insurance coverage appliesThe central question was whether clauses 34 and 35 required the loss or damage itself to occur within the relevant period, or whether it was enough that the underlying defect or cause arose within that period, even if the insured's loss was suffered later. Mr Fall-Armytage acquired title well after the two years for non-structural defects had expired. At first instance, the County Court judge considered the point finely balanced. The judge concluded that the words "occurring during the period" in clause 34 were more naturally read as referring to the immediately preceding words, namely the non-structural defect. The judge accepted that this created a long-tail liability for the insurer but regarded the outcome as compelled by the text.Niall CJ, McLeish JA and Whelan JA rejected that construction. They held that clauses 34 and 35 are concerned with when the insured's loss, damage or expense occurs, not merely when the underlying defect or cause arises. According to Cogent Legal, the Court found the answer in the policy's text and structure: both clauses sat under the heading "How long are you covered for?" The punctuation and grammar of clause 35 showed that the temporal phrase referred to "loss, damage or expense" rather than the cause; and clause 32 indemnified loss or damage sustained by the insured. Cogent Legal adds that the Court treated broad appeals to commercial purpose and consumer protection as too general to resolve the question, and that the ministerial order made under section 135 of the Building Act 1993 (Vic) prescribed minimum cover only.How did section 9 affect the homeowner’s building insurance claimMr Fall-Armytage also advanced a notice of contention. He argued that, even on the insurer's construction, the loss had occurred within the period of cover because the original owner suffered loss when the defective work was completed. He relied on section 9 of the Domestic Building Contracts Act 1995 (Vic), under which warranties under section 8 run with the building and may be enforced by the owner for the time being as if that person were a party to the contract. The Court of Appeal rejected the argument. It held that sections 8 and 9 create statutory warranties and overcome privity, but do not authorise a successor in title to recover for loss or damage suffered by a previous owner. In the article's words, "Section 9 gives standing." A later owner must still prove their own loss, which the article describes as a question of fact that may depend on matters such as whether the defect was known at the time of purchase and whether the purchase price reflected it.On the outcome, the Court of Appeal granted leave to appeal and allowed the appeal. The trial judge's orders were set aside and replaced with orders dismissing Mr Fall-Armytage's claim, except in relation to the 11th defect. The Court still had to classify that defect as structural or non-structural, and it remitted the issue to the County Court for further hearing and determination, as it was not in a position to decide it on the record before it. The Court expressed the hope that, given the small amount involved, the issue might be resolved by agreement. The decision is Victorian Building Authority v Fall-Armytage [2026] VSCA 32.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2009, families in Long Branch, New Jersey, forced the city to withdraw takeover cases that would have cleared their modest homes for luxury condominiums
articles.summary: In a landmark decision, families in Long Branch, New Jersey succeeded in protecting their homes from eminent domain actions aimed at clearing land for luxury condominiums, ending years of legal disputes and establishing vital protections for neighborhood residents.
articles.body: Families in Long Branch, New Jersey spent years fighting the city’s attempt to acquire their homes through eminent domain for a private redevelopment project. The dispute concluded in September 2009, with an agreement that dismissed the condemnation cases, protecting homeowners from future takings under redevelopment plans to the neighbourhood.The neighborhood, known as MTOTSA, covered Marine Terrace, Ocean Terrace and Seaview Avenue had families for generations as occupants of its cottages and bungalows. Among them was Lori Vendetti, whose parents, Carmen and Josephine Venditti, as a summer residence built their MTOTSA home in 1960 and eventually retired there in 1989. Lori lived across the street from her parent’s house.The MTOTSA neighbourhood was designated by Long Branch as part of a required redevelopment in 1996. However, representatives of several homeowners; the Institute for Justice argued that the neighborhood didn’t meet the conditions associated with blight. A city survey that year found only three of 38 residences, or 7.8%, in poor condition. In their argument, the organization pointed to a 1995 plan which recommended the preservation of MTOTSA and to a statement from Mayor Adam Schneider in 2001 which deemed that the neighborhood to be in good condition.The redevelopment plan moved toward private residential constructionThe city gave the contract of redevelopment to Applied Companies in February 2000 and later partnered with Matzel & Mumford, a subsidiary of K. Hovnanian. The plans submitted in 2004 called for 150 condominiums and townhouses, and the proposed selling prices ranged from $500,000 to more than $1 million. However, the plan was later amended and the number of units was increased to 185, rendering the estimated potential revenue from the project to reach $130 million to $185 million.The city filed eminent-domain actions against homeowners in 2005 and 2006. In June 2006, A Monmouth County Superior Court ruling allowed the condemnation effort to proceed. The homeowners appealed with representation from the Institute for Justice and New Jersey attorney Peter Wegener.In August 2008, a three-judge panel of the New Jersey Appellate Division unanimously reversed the lower-court decision. The panel found that substantial evidence was not provided by Long Branch to support its findings that properties required redevelopment on the basis asserted by the city which sent the case back to the trial court. Subsequently, Long Branch indicated that it was willing to withdraw the eminent-domain actions, and negotiations began over the remaining issues surrounding the neighborhood.The September 2009 agreement ended the condemnation cases The agreement gave homeowners access to tax abatements allowing them to reinvest in their properties, while part of their attorneys’ fees was paid for by the city. In addition, it also required Long Branch to repave and repair all streets in the neighborhood, along with long-neglected streetlights. The settlement addressed developer-owned properties as well, some had been abandoned and boarded up. The developer was required to begin the work immediately and complete demolition of those homes by April 2, 2010. The court retained jurisdiction over the agreement to ensure that its terms were carried out. For Lori Vendetti and other residents, the settlement concluded the immediate threat of losing their homes through the condemnation cases. In a victory announcement in November 2009, Vendetti said, “At long last, we can get our homes, lives and neighborhood back.” as reported by the Institute of Justice.The Long Branch case unfolded at the backdrop of a wider legal debate concerning eminent domain after the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2005 decision in Kelo v. City of New London. The case concerned the government’s extent to use eminent domain for private development based on expected economic benefits. In Long Branch, however, the 2008 appellate ruling focused specifically on the evidence supporting the city’s redevelopment and blight findings. The 2009 agreement then ended the condemnation actions and established protections for the MTOTSA homeowners.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'BSP is my family': Akash Anand's fresh appeal to Mayawati after BSP exit
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: \"Respected Bahanji, I am not going to any other political party. Not today, not ever.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: "Respected Bahanji, I am not going to any other political party. Not today, not ever. The BSP is not just a party for me; it is my family." Akash Anand's declaration on Friday comes after weeks of uncertainty over his political future and nearly three weeks after Mayawati first removed him as the BSP's national coordinator and then completely relieved him from the party on September 10.His latest message is seen as an attempt to make his position clear, but it also directly addresses the issue that became central to Mayawati's decision: his silence when she asked his father-in-law, Ashok Siddharth, to retire from politics.Anand's expulsion was the latest turn in a political relationship that had already seen repeated reversals.He had been expelled from the BSP in May 2024 and again in March 2025, only to be taken back within a month on both occasions and subsequently given important responsibilities. Last month, Mayawati removed him from the post of national coordinator, saying he needed greater political maturity and would not be entrusted with major organisational responsibilities for the time being.READ ALSO: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay plays bus conductor, hands out tickets after expanding free travel schemeThe repost that became a loyalty testThe immediate trigger for the final break was Anand's failure to repost a statement made by Mayawati on September 9.In a post on X, Mayawati had said that if Siddharth genuinely wanted what was best for his son-in-law, he should take complete political retirement so that Anand could work freely in the BSP. Anand did not repost the statement.Mayawati specifically pointed to the silence because, according to her, Anand had earlier reposted her statements to demonstrate his loyalty. This time, however, the statement concerned his father-in-law as well as Anand's own political future.For Mayawati, the omission appeared to signify something larger. She said Anand remained more strongly attached to his family relationship with Siddharth than to the BSP and its movement. She questioned how he could effectively work for the party while remaining divided between familial ties and the organisation's interests.Siddharth's retirement did not bring Anand backSiddharth subsequently announced his retirement from politics on September 10. Mayawati described his decision as appropriate but also said it had come late.Rather than restoring Anand's position, she announced that he too would be completely relieved from the BSP. She maintained that both Anand and Siddharth had shown greater attachment to personal and familial interests than to the party and its broader mission.The sequence was significant. Siddharth's retirement, which had been presented as the condition that could allow Anand to work freely in the party, did not lead to Anand's restoration. Instead, it was followed by the final break.Anand now gives his versionAnand's Friday post directly addresses that sequence. He called Mayawati his "political guru", his "inspiration" and his paternal aunt, saying that everything he had learnt in politics had come from her and everything he had done had been under her guidance.He then addressed the speculation surrounding his political future, making an emphatic declaration that he would not join another party."The BSP is not just a party for me; it is my family," he said, while also placing his latest appeal directly before Mayawati and the wider Bahujan community.Crucially, Anand also backed Mayawati's decision concerning Siddharth. He said her decision to expel his father-in-law and his subsequent political renunciation was "entirely appropriate" and that he stood by it."Relationships have their place, but the mission is greater than them," Anand said, adding that it was his responsibility to place the interests of the party and the movement above personal and familial interests.His explanation for the missing repostAnand also offered an explanation for the very silence that Mayawati had interpreted as a sign of divided loyalty.He said that at the time he had distanced himself from social media and therefore could not repost Mayawati's post. According to Anand, his silence was subsequently misunderstood and created space for rumours about his political future."If this has hurt you, then I seek forgiveness from you," he said.The apology is central to Anand's latest attempt to repair his relationship with Mayawati. Rather than challenging her interpretation of his silence, he acknowledged that it had caused hurt and sought forgiveness.The request behind the apologyAnand's post ultimately goes beyond denying rumours or explaining his social media absence. The post is seen as an attempt to seek another political opportunity."I only seek the opportunity to serve the party and the mission again under your leadership," he said, adding that trust is not built through words but through actions. He promised to prove himself through his conduct and hard work.He ended by defining his politics through three references: Baba Saheb's mission, Manyavar Saheb's path and Mayawati's leadership.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: A New Jersey homebuyer rejected 10 older houses, then negotiated a $575,000 Pennsylvania new build down to $545,000 and used $30,000 in builder incentives to cut his mortgage rate from 6.25% to 5.25%, saving about $350 a month
articles.summary: Jonathan Ayala began looking for a home in Hoboken, New Jersey, without considering new construction.
articles.body: Jonathan Ayala began looking for a home in Hoboken, New Jersey, without considering new construction. The real estate agent and owner of a photography and marketing business instead focused on the costs involved in buying and owning a property. After viewing 10 homes in person, however, he found that none made enough financial sense to buy.Ayala looked beyond the asking prices of the properties. He also considered their condition, the repairs and upgrades they might need, and the financing involved. “I wanted to see the condition of each property, what repairs and upgrades were recommended, and the financing and overall cost of owning each property,” he says, as quoted by Realtor.com.Some of the older homes needed major work. Several required new roofs, while one had water damage. Ayala realised that negotiating a lower purchase price would not necessarily make those properties a better deal if he still had to spend heavily on repairs before moving in.“It was both exciting and frustrating,” Ayala says of the house hunt, which lasted roughly a month. As he compared each property, the search increasingly became a calculation of the asking price against the cost of repairs, renovations and future maintenance.“These homes were appealing at first, but all the repair, renovation and maintenance and other costs can add up fast,” he says. That calculation changed when a newly built home appeared within the price range he had been considering.A new construction changes calculationAyala found a three-bedroom, 2.5-bathroom townhouse in Easton, Pennsylvania. The new-construction property was listed for $575,000. Rather than simply accepting the listed price, he began discussions with the builder about the terms of a possible purchase.Those discussions introduced another part of the calculation: builder incentives. Ayala says the incentives were not offered immediately, but he eventually secured a package worth $30,000.To receive the full incentive package, Ayala had to use the builder’s preferred lender and title company. The $30,000 was split between different parts of the purchase rather than being given as a single reduction in the sale price.“For me, the $30,000 was a more meaningful incentive because it lowered several real costs of the home purchase versus just a headline number.”The package included $15,000 towards closing costs, $10,000 towards a mortgage-rate buydown and $5,000 for interior finish upgrades. The mortgage-rate buydown was particularly important to Ayala because it reduced the rate from a possible 6.25% to 5.25%.Mortgage rate falls from 6.25% to 5.25%The lower mortgage rate changed the monthly cost of the purchase. Ayala says the buydown reduced his monthly principal and interest payments by about $350 compared with the rate he would otherwise have received.“This lowered my monthly principal and interest payments by about $350 compared to the rate I would have received,” he says.The purchase price also changed during negotiations. Ayala was able to bring the price of the townhouse down from $575,000 to $545,000.He put down $109,000, which was 20% of the purchase price. Following the down payment, his monthly mortgage payment was $2,408.With both the purchase price and financing terms on the table, Ayala went back to the comparison that had shaped his original search. He looked again at the older homes he had already visited and considered what each would have cost after repairs and other work.“I did a much closer comparison with the pre-existing homes that I had already looked at and was considering—that’s when the offer became that much more interesting.”He wanted to see the finished propertyThe financial terms were important, but Ayala also wanted to make sure the finished townhouse matched what he was actually considering buying. He returned to the builder and toured a townhouse that had already been completed.That allowed him to see the finished property instead of relying only on a model home. “I was able to evaluate the actual finished property and that was important to me,” he says. “I didn’t want to make a decision based on the appeal of a model home. I wanted to make a decision based on what I would actually purchase. Walking through the finished home gave me a real feeling of it; it was not a leap of faith,” he says.Once the price and other terms were agreed, Ayala says the transaction and closing went smoothly. The decision also left him satisfied with the overall deal. “There’s no question I got a much better package overall by buying new construction.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Rafale, F-15EX & Gripen: Why 4th gen jets are bagging billion-dollar orders in age of 6th-gen fighters
articles.summary: Even as the world's air forces race towards fifth- and sixth-generation stealth fighters, a parallel and equally significant trend is unfolding; nation
articles.body: Even as the world's air forces race towards fifth- and sixth-generation stealth fighters, a parallel and equally significant trend is unfolding; nation after nation continues to place large orders for fourth- and 4.5-generation aircraft.France's Rafale, the US F-15EX and several other platforms are still attracting major orders, with order books for these fighters swelling even as cutting-edge stealth programmes dominate the headlines.France's Dassault Rafale had crossed 200 aircraft on order as of early 2026, with Indonesia beginning deliveries this year under its 2022 order for 42 jets. Ukraine, meanwhile, has disclosed plans to acquire Rafale F4s as part of a broader French defence package, although a firm contract has yet to be signed. The US Air Force has also expanded its planned F-15EX Eagle II fleet, with a $2.38 billion contract for 22 additional jets signed in September. Saudi Arabia and Qatar are also evaluating the modernised F-15, while Japan, South Korea and Singapore remain among its established international operators.Sweden's Gripen E/F has also secured fresh interest across Latin America. Peru selected the fighter for a proposed $3.5 billion deal covering 24 jets in 2025, although a contract has yet to be signed. Colombia has signed a roughly $1.9 billion contract for up to 17 aircraft, while Brazil is reportedly in talks over a follow-on purchase. Ukraine has also committed to acquiring the Gripen under a 2025 letter of intent.The Eurofighter Typhoon had more than 150 aircraft in its order backlog as of June 2026, with Turkey among the countries discussing a potential acquisition.So why are these supposedly "outdated" fourth-generation fighters still in demand?Cost is a major factor. They are generally cheaper to acquire, operate and maintain than fifth-generation fighters. They also offer high availability, backed by decades of operational experience and continuous upgrades. Many of today's fourth-generation platforms are equipped with advanced radars, modern avionics, sophisticated electronic warfare systems and long-range weapons such as the Meteor beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile, narrowing much of the capability gap with newer fighters at a significantly lower cost.Their ability to carry large external weapon loads is another advantage. Fifth-generation fighters can also carry weapons externally, but doing so increases their radar signature and compromises one of their biggest advantages: stealth. Fourth-generation fighters face no such constraint and can carry substantial weapons loads for missions ranging from air-to-ground strikes to maritime attack.Their flexibility and relatively lower operating costs also make them attractive to countries looking to build up air combat capacity or replace ageing fleets. Crucially, many of these aircraft are available now, while newer-generation programmes can take years to develop, produce and scale up.That does not mean fourth-generation fighters are without serious limitations. Their larger radar cross-section makes them more vulnerable in heavily defended and contested airspace, where stealth aircraft can operate with greater survivability. They also generally lack the level of sensor fusion and networked situational awareness that has become a defining feature of fifth-generation fighters.But that does not make them obsolete. Instead, air forces are increasingly looking at fourth- and fifth-generation fighters as complementary capabilities. Stealth aircraft can penetrate heavily defended airspace, conduct high-value missions and suppress or disrupt enemy air defences, while fourth-generation fighters provide greater numbers, heavier weapons loads and the capacity to handle a broader range of missions at a more sustainable cost.As defence budgets are stretched between maintaining existing fleets and funding increasingly expensive next-generation programmes, the fourth-generation fighter is proving remarkably resilient. It may no longer represent the technological cutting edge, but it remains a capable, flexible and relatively affordable workhorse that can operate alongside the stealth fleets of tomorrow.

articles.title: Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar's wife recalls shock: 'Didn't have the mental capacity'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Sonal Machchhar, wife of Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, recalled the horrifying moment she learnt about the mid-air attack on her husband
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Sonal Machchhar, wife of Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, recalled the horrifying moment she learnt about the mid-air attack on her husband aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, saying she was "very devastated" and did not have the immediate "mental capacity" to comprehend the crisis.In a conversation with a news channel, Sonal described being overcome with shock after hearing the news, news agency ANI reported."I was very devastated. And I didn’t have the mental capacity (to know) how I should react," she said.She said the presence of friends and family, along with updates from Indian authorities, offered her reassurance during the ordeal."But as I had my friends and family around me, I was reassured that everything is okay. And very soon, I started getting news that he is stable," she said.Sonal met her husband on Thursday at a hospital in Abu Dhabi, which helped ease her concerns about his condition, ANI reported.Reflecting on the meeting, she said, "I met him on Thursday, and that gives me reassurance that he is in the right hands, very good care, under the good care of UAE doctors, military doctors."Sonal said her immediate focus was on helping her husband recover. "And I’m just hoping that he comes back home soon, and I’m going to do whatever it takes for his recovery," she said.Asked about reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wanted to speak with Captain Machchhar, Sonal said the conversation should take place directly between them once her husband has recovered sufficiently, ANI reported."I will not be able to talk to Mr Netanyahu. I think Smit is the right person; he should answer to Mr Netanyahu," she said, adding that "he will definitely talk to him once he is in the right frame of mind."Earlier on Friday, Captain Machchhar spoke to Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the phone and recalled the moments after he collapsed on the floor following the attack.He said his 17 years of flying experience helped him realise that the aircraft was going down.The captain said that while he was consciously telling himself that he was acting for his own survival, he knew deep down that he could not allow the passengers to die.The Prime Minister praised Machchhar's courage, patience and presence of mind and said his actions had made the country proud, ANI reported.The September 30 security crisis involved a flydubai flight operating from Dubai to Tel Aviv, where the Omani co-pilot allegedly stabbed the commander in an apparent terror-driven attempt to bring down the plane.The confrontation triggered a steep descent, with the aircraft dropping approximately 16,000 feet within two minutes before a hijacking distress signal was transmitted.Despite sustaining severe injuries, Captain Machchhar resisted the assailant.Flight crew members and passengers then breached the flight deck and restrained the attacker, allowing the crew to regain control of the aircraft.The plane subsequently made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where all 180 occupants disembarked safely, ANI reported.The captain managed to repel the co-pilot sufficiently to unlatch the cockpit entry, while two non-duty aviators on board assumed control of the aircraft for its emergency landing in Tabuk.The identity of the co-pilot has not been publicly disclosed.The co-pilot was transferred to the UAE after his arrest.Israeli investigative personnel have also been sent to the UAE to join the locally led inquiry and help determine whether outside parties orchestrated the attack.(With agency inputs)You Can articles.title: Michigan's $3.219 billion Soo Locks project has reached 50% of its final phase, on track for completion by 2030; crews will use 400,000 cubic yards of concrete, enough for a sidewalk from Sault Ste. Marie to Orlando
articles.summary: Michigan’s Soo Locks project has reached 50% completion in its final construction phase, according to the US Army Corps of Engineers. On Tuesday, Sept.
articles.body: Michigan’s Soo Locks project has reached 50% completion in its final construction phase, according to the US Army Corps of Engineers. On Tuesday, Sept. 29, it confirmed that the $3.219 billion project remains on track to be completed by 2030.This marks a significant milestone for the project, which kicked off in 2020. The 50% figure applies to Phase 3 alone. Phase 1, the upstream channel deepening, wrapped up in 2022. Phase 2, the upstream approach walls, followed in 2024. The final phase of the project is being carried out by joint-venture contractor Kokosing Alberici Traylor LLC, known as KAT, which signed the contract in July 2022. The Corps awarded the last remaining contract options in June 2025, and KAT has completed $975 million worth of work through the end of August.“Reaching the halfway point on this mega project is a testament to the dedication of the Corps of Engineers team and the joint-venture contractor Kokosing Alberici Traylor LLC (KAT). The progress made here is a direct reflection of the more than 600 people working on this project. They come to work every day committed to the successful completion of the new lock,” Corps of Engineers Integrated Project Office Chief Mick Awbrey told WXYZ-TV.Phase 3 is a significant part of the construction. Crews are building “cofferdams at each end of the lock, demolishing the existing Sabin Lock, filling in the existing Davis Lock, excavating bedrock, constructing the New Lock chamber walls and floor, fabrication and installation of miter gates, installation of mechanical and electrical systems, installation of an innovative hands-free mooring system, rehabilitating the downstream approach walls and constructing a new pump well”.At present, the focus is on the concrete. The mass concrete placement for the concrete walls, the lock floor and the new pump well is underway, with more than 600 people on the job. Steel structures are being fabricated offsite in parallel. The finished lock will take roughly 400,000 cubic yards.“If you were to build an average sidewalk that you see in a neighbourhood, with 400,000 cubic yards of concrete, you could build a sidewalk from Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, to Orlando, Florida. It’s a massive amount of concrete, and we are making progress every day,” Awbrey told the broadcaster. Through August, crews had placed 140,198 cubic yards, about 35% of the total. On the sidewalk map, that gets them almost to Dayton, Ohio.The new lock will match the Poe’s dimensions: 1,200 feet long, 110 feet wide and 32 feet deep. It is going up in the footprint of the Sabin Lock, which is coming down. The Corps ranks it among the highest-priority commercial navigation projects in the country. A second Poe-sized lock adds resilience to a facility that now leans on one, keeping raw materials moving to steel producers and protecting thousands of jobs, it argues. The agency also calls the project a flagship of its ‘Building Infrastructure, Not Paperwork’ initiative, which it describes as delivering faster and at lower cost.You use AI every day.
